CausalChain: RMDN1 upregulation -> Recruitment of HDAC1 and assembly of repressive complexes (including CoREST and interactions with KRT19/SMARCB1 modules) -> Inhibition of EP300-mediated acetylation -> Decreased chromatin accessibility at pro-metastatic/angiogenic gene loci (and modulation of miRNA silencing) -> Reduced activation of oncogenic programs -> Mitigation of metastasis and improved liver neoplasm prognosis
Hypothesis: We hypothesize that in liver neoplasms, upregulation of RMDN1 acts as a master regulator of chromatin dynamics by orchestrating a composite epigenetic repression mechanism. RMDN1 achieves this by recruiting HDAC1 and facilitating the formation of repressive complexes that include elements of the CoREST complex and previously characterized modulators such as KRT19 and SMARCB1. This coordinated assembly effectively counteracts the histone acetylation function of EP300, leading to decreased accessibility and transcriptional activity of genes that drive metastasis and angiogenesis. Moreover, RMDN1 may exert additional control by impacting locus-specific regulatory regions, including miRNA promoters such as that of miR-493-5p, thereby ensuring robust silencing of pro-oncogenic targets. Contemporary methods like CRISPR-based epigenome editing, single-cell ATAC-seq, and spatial transcriptomics will be employed to validate the physical interactions and functional consequences of this regulatory cascade, offering precise insights into its role in mitigating liver neoplasm aggressiveness.
Abstract: In liver neoplasms, we propose that increased expression of RMDN1 initiates a novel epigenetic regulatory mechanism that integrates traditional chromatin repression with additional layers of gene regulation. Specifically, RMDN1 not only recruits chromatin repressor proteins such as HDAC1 to counteract the acetyltransferase activity of EP300 but also modulates a broader regulatory network, potentially involving the CoREST complex, KRT19-associated HDAC1 recruitment, and SMARCB1-mediated EP300 interactions. This integrated network leads to decreased chromatin accessibility at pro-metastatic and pro-angiogenic gene loci. Furthermore, RMDN1 may influence locus-specific epigenetic silencing events, such as miRNA deregulation (e.g., miR-493-5p), thereby reinforcing transcriptional repression. We propose to leverage contemporary technologies including CRISPR-based epigenome editing, single-cell ATAC-seq, and spatial transcriptomics to dissect the molecular underpinnings and validate this multifaceted regulatory axis. This approach not only refines the mechanistic insights into RMDN1’s role in liver neoplasm progression but also provides innovative avenues for targeted therapeutic interventions.
Orignal_vs_New: The new hypothesis explicitly retains the original causal chain in that it posits RMDN1 upregulation leads to recruitment of chromatin repressors (HDAC1) which then counteracts the activity of the chromatin activator EP300, resulting in decreased activation of pro-metastatic genes and suppressed tumor progression. However, it extends this model by integrating additional regulatory elements such as the CoREST complex, KRT19, SMARCB1, and locus-specific miRNA silencing (e.g., miR-493-5p) to provide a more comprehensive regulatory framework. Furthermore, it improves practical implementability by incorporating modern technological approaches (CRISPR-based epigenome editing, single-cell ATAC-seq, spatial transcriptomics) to enable detailed experimental validation and mechanistic exploration of the proposed regulatory axis.
